other_side: Zitron, writing eight days earlier on the amended filing, treats the falling valuation not as noise but as one sign among several that the money is running out. He argues Anthropic has committed to about $447.5 billion of compute spending before the end of 2030, expects a junk credit rating, and will have to borrow at eight to eleven per cent to cover the gap. He says its obligations are "priced for perfection", requiring it to double in a year, while Ramp expects fourth-quarter growth of only 15 to 25 per cent. He also claims around four fifths of its revenue comes from venture-backed startups, so growth depends on venture capital continuing to flow.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether Anthropic's revenue can keep growing faster than the fixed compute bills it has signed. Both accept the filed numbers: a price range implying about $1.25 to $1.4 trillion, run-rate revenue in the tens of billions, and several hundred billion dollars of commitments falling due by 2030. The empirical question is whether growth holds once those payments start. The observables are the first public quarterly results, fourth-quarter growth against Ramp's forecast of 15 to 25 per cent, and the interest rate on any debt Anthropic raises. The residue is worldview: whether demand for AI labour is durable, or on loan from venture capital. For Whittemore to be vindicated, revenue must broaden beyond coding into finance, law and life sciences, and the shares must hold. For Zitron, growth must stall while costs rise and lenders balk. Both are polemicists with incentives, Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both say today's figures cannot tell you what this company is worth. Watch the first day of trading next week.
